\textbf{Re: Submission of an original research article,} ``Predicting breast cancer grade from routine
clinical data: an open multi-cohort study with transport to Saudi patients''

Dear Editor-in-Chief,

I am pleased to submit the above manuscript for consideration as a full-length research article in
\emph{Computers in Biology and Medicine}.

Histological grade is one of the strongest prognostic factors in breast cancer, yet it is assigned
only after tissue examination and is only moderately reproducible between pathologists. Machine-learning
studies increasingly try to predict grade from images, but there is no transparent, externally validated
baseline showing how much grade the routine clinical record already carries. Such studies are also
exposed to data leakage, because public breast cancer datasets contain variables that encode grade.
Finally, it is unknown whether models developed on Western data give correct predictions for patients in
Saudi Arabia, where breast cancer presents younger and is more often hormone-receptor-negative.

To address these gaps, we built an open, checksummed data model of \NGradedTotal{} grade-labelled
invasive breast cancers from \NGradedCohorts{} public cohorts. We then compared seven models, from a
prevalence baseline to gradient boosting, with nested cross-validation and frozen validation in five
external cohorts on three continents. The main findings are:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt,topsep=2pt]
\item Routine variables predict grade moderately and consistently (macro-AUC \IntAucMinR--\IntAucMaxR{}
internally; \ExtAucMin--\ExtAucMax{} externally). Gradient boosting did not improve on logistic
regression (difference \XgbDeltaInt, 95\% CI \XgbDeltaIntLo{} to \XgbDeltaIntHi).
\item Predictor effects transported across cohorts, but calibration did not: the same model
under-predicted grade~3 in one cohort and over-predicted it in another. A simple intercept update
corrected both.
\item Common leakage shortcuts inflated apparent performance by up to \LeakMaxInfl{} in macro-AUC, more
than the gap between a useless and the best correctly validated model.
\item In \NDukeRad{} patients with breast MRI, 529 radiomic features did not improve on the routine
clinical variables.
\item Re-weighting the cohorts to published Saudi case-mix showed that Western-trained models would
over-predict high-grade disease in Saudi patients, so local recalibration is essential.
\end{itemize}

We believe the work fits the journal's scope in computational methods for medicine, and it offers
four things that readers will find useful. It provides a reproducible benchmark that image-based grading
tools can be measured against. It shows that a simple, interpretable model is sufficient. It gives
concrete evidence of how leakage inflates results. And it offers practical guidance on recalibrating
models before they are used in a new population.

The study is reported according to TRIPOD+AI (prediction) and STROBE (descriptive analyses); the
completed TRIPOD+AI checklist is included in the supplementary material. It uses only de-identified, publicly released data, so no ethics approval
was required. All code, configuration files and results are available in an anonymised repository
[insert anonymous repository link]. A single command reproduces every table, figure and number in the
manuscript.

I confirm that this manuscript is original, has not been published previously, and is not under
consideration for publication elsewhere. [All authors have approved the submission.] The author
declares no competing interests and received no specific funding for this work [confirm]. The use of
